posts.title: Change the spec, not the code
posts.media: One word changed in Button's spec: Figma and code each get their instructions from it, and change together
posts.text: We changed one word in a file, and our Button changed in Figma and in code. That file is the Button's spec. It says, once, what the button is made of and which token each part uses. Figma and code each get their instructions from it, so when it changes, both change. Nobody re-types anything. That's how we keep Figma and code from drifting apart at Nagarro: there's only one place to make a change. And until Figma catches up, a check reads the Figma file and says exactly which layer is behind. Most teams keep two libraries in step by hand. Where does your source of truth live? #designsystems #figma #designops
posts.notes: Everything in the clip is real: a throwaway copy of the repo, the CSS the real ds:generate wrote, two Figma exports before and after the bind snippet on a scratch copy. The clip shows the Secondary Button because Primary currently differs between Figma (purple) and code (blue): check which is right before posting a Primary side by side.

posts.title: Token names say the job, not the value
posts.text: Quick test: what does blue-500 do? You can't tell. It describes a look, not a job, so every designer and developer decides again where it goes. In the design systems we build at Nagarro, every token name says its job, in up to five words, always in the same order: color/background/interactive/primary/hover Swipe for the grammar, and the one rule that says no. What's the hardest word your team ever had to agree on? #designsystems #designtokens #figma
posts.notes: The grammar is in docs/Tokens-semantic-v2.xlsx (Vocabulary tab); every example name is a real token. The carousel is carousels/token-names.md.

posts.title: Status colors start neutral
posts.media: Toasts of each type: status color has a place, not a fixed hue
posts.text: Unpopular opinion: your design system shouldn't decide that error is red. Red, amber and green are a product decision. A bank, a hospital and a game use them differently, and some brands are red to begin with. So in the starter we build client systems from at Nagarro, status colors start neutral. What the system does decide is where status color goes: a subtle background, a border, an icon. Pick the palette later and every typed component follows. Opinionated about structure. Neutral about taste. #designsystems #uxdesign #designtokens
posts.notes: The clip is the real Toast component in Storybook.

posts.title: Accessibility before the audit
posts.media: A brand color too light to read: the warning, and readable shades of it
posts.text: I typed a sunny yellow as our brand color. The design system pushed back. 1.4:1 against the page. Buttons need 3:1. Then it offered readable shades of the same yellow, one click away. That's how we think about accessibility at Nagarro: as close to the decision as possible. In our starter, contrast is checked while you pick colors, and again on every pull request, for every brand, in light and dark. An audit at the end finds problems. Checks while you design prevent them. #accessibility #designsystems #a11y
posts.notes: Filmed live in the configurator (Edit theme, Brand color #FFD43B). The ratio in the caption is read from the warning itself.

posts.title: The tokens we almost deleted
posts.media: Picture: Unused is not unneeded, a rule from our token vocabulary
posts.text: We almost deleted half our design tokens. Nothing used them. It looked tidy. It would have been a mistake. A new system has hundreds of tokens and a handful of components. The tokens aren't unneeded: the components that need them just don't exist yet. Delete them, and the next person invents their own. Two names for one job. That's where drift starts. So it's a rule in our token vocabulary at Nagarro now: unused is not unneeded. A token only goes when it breaks a naming rule. What did your design system learn the hard way? #designsystems #designtokens #designops
posts.notes: A still picture; the names on it are real tokens. Tell it the way you remember it.

posts.title: AI can only follow what it can read
posts.media: Asking the design system a question: the answer comes from its own docs
posts.text: Ask a general AI to build a screen for your product and it guesses. A button from some popular library. A color that's close enough. So we asked our design system instead. The specs that generate our components also write a guide for AI: every component, its props, its tokens, when to use which. Ask "Which button should a table row use for Remove?" and the answer comes from the system's own rules. AI is only as consistent as what it can read. Write your decisions down where people and machines can both find them. #designsystems #ai #designops
posts.notes: Filmed live; the answer is the agent's, on the starter system's own docs (llms.txt and docs/ai/). The wait is sped up, and the clip says so.

posts.title: One decision, many variables
posts.media: Restyling GitHub's Primer: one brand decision turns out to be two
posts.text: Field notes: we tried to rebrand GitHub's Primer from one brand color. It didn't work, and that was the interesting part. In Primer, "brand" only covers the green primary button. Links, focus rings and checked controls use a separate blue accent. Change the brand alone and you get a purple button next to blue links. Our configurator's agent spotted it by reading Primer's own variables and guides, and showed brand and accent as the two decisions they really are. If you're inheriting a design system: map its decisions, not just its variables. #designsystems #designtokens #theming
posts.notes: From a real run. Primer is public and well made: describe, never criticise.

posts.title: Start from the system you have
posts.media: Loading a design system that already exists: GitHub's Primer, read in seconds
posts.text: Most companies that ask us about a design system already have one. Starting over is rarely the answer. The first job is understanding what's there: which components exist in code, which in Figma, and where the two quietly disagree. So at Nagarro we start by reading it. Point at the repo and the Storybook, and in seconds its own components are live, with its docs and tokens found. An agent keeps checking it in the background and maps its Figma file to its code. An audit doesn't have to start with weeks of spreadsheets. It can start with a map. #designsystems #designops #figma
posts.notes: The clip is the loading recording with captions; the agent's wait is sped up. The Figma mapping needs a Figma token and isn't in the clip.

posts.title: Dark mode isn't a second design
posts.media: Light and dark: the same components and token names, other values
posts.text: How many screens has your team designed twice? Once light, once dark? Dark mode isn't a second design. It's a second set of values. In the systems we build at Nagarro, components never point at a color. They point at a name, like color/background/surface/low. Light and dark give that name different values. Flip the switch and everything follows, together. If your dark mode lives on a separate Figma page, it will drift from the light one. Every time. #designsystems #darkmode #designtokens
posts.notes: Filmed live on the starter's components page. color/background/surface/low is a real token.

posts.title: A second brand without a fork
posts.media: Two brands and two modes on the same components
posts.text: A client asks for a second brand. The old answer: copy the component library and maintain two. Ours: one system, one set of components, and a brand that only owns what's different. Its colors, its fonts or its shape. In the video, Acme Health gets a sister brand, Acme Kids, in light and dark. Same components, same token names. In Figma each brand is its own variable collection, so designers switch brands like they switch modes. How many copies of your component library exist right now? #designsystems #branding #designops
posts.notes: Acme Health is a made-up client; say so if asked.

posts.title: Corners are a decision
posts.media: One corner decision, and every component follows
posts.text: Sharp. Round. Extra round. Corner radius looks like a detail. In a design system it's one decision that touches every button, field, card and dialog. So we make it once. In our starter at Nagarro, one roundness setting drives every corner token, on a 4px grid, in code and, through our plugin, in Figma. If changing your corners means a ticket per component, your system is storing answers instead of decisions. #designsystems #uidesign #designtokens
posts.notes: Filmed live in Edit theme → Radius.

posts.title: Every state has a name
posts.media: A button in each of its states, each one a named token
posts.text: Default. Hover. Pressed. Disabled. Four states of one button. In many teams that's four hex codes in a handover file, and four chances to guess. In the systems we build at Nagarro, every state has a name: color/background/interactive/primary/hover color/background/interactive/primary/pressed Designers pick the name in Figma. Developers use the same name in CSS. Nobody types a hex code. It quietly removes a whole category of "which blue was it?" messages. #designsystems #designtokens #frontend
posts.notes: The clip is the real Button in Storybook; the names in its captions are real tokens.

posts.title: Press Tab
posts.media: Tabbing through a form: the focus ring is part of the design
posts.text: Try this on your product today: put the mouse away and press Tab. Can you always see where you are? For keyboard users, the focus ring is the cursor. It's one of the most used parts of any interface, and one of the least designed. In the components we build at Nagarro, the focus outline is a design token like any other, so it gets the same care as a brand color, in every brand and mode. Somebody navigates your product this way every day. Design for them on purpose. #accessibility #a11y #designsystems
posts.notes: The clip tabs through the real Form component in Storybook.

posts.title: The handover is the bug
posts.media: The questions every handover asks, answered by one token name
posts.text: "What's the hover color?" "The blue one." "Which blue?" If this happens in your team every sprint, the handover isn't the problem. The missing names are. Our design systems at Nagarro use the same token names in Figma and in code. A developer inspecting a button in Figma's Dev Mode sees color/background/interactive/primary/hover, and that exact name is in the CSS. The best handover is the one with nothing left to ask. #designsystems #designhandoff #figma
posts.notes: The clip is an animation; the conversation is made up, the name is a real token.

posts.title: Docs that can't go stale
posts.media: The documentation beside each Figma component, generated from its spec
posts.text: Every design system has a docs page that was right once. Docs go stale because they're written separately from the thing they describe. Ours aren't. Each component is described once, in a spec: parts, variants, tokens, usage. The docs panel beside each component in our Figma library is built from that spec, and so is its page on the site. Change the spec, and the docs rebuild. Documentation shouldn't be a chore someone forgets. It should be a by-product. #designsystems #documentation #figma
posts.notes: The clip pans over the real Figma capture. The plugin rebuilds the panels from the specs.

posts.title: Drift has a number
posts.media: The check that reads the Figma file and names every layer that drifted
posts.text: How far apart are your Figma library and your code right now? Most teams answer with a feeling. We answer with a number. A script reads our Figma file layer by layer and compares every variant with its component's spec. Today: 53 / 56 components match, and for the rest it names the exact layer and the token it expected. Drift you can measure is drift you can fix this week, not next quarter. #designsystems #figma #designops
posts.notes: The clip shows the real output of ds:parity on the day it was filmed. Film it again after fixing the differences.

posts.title: I built the tool behind our videos
posts.byline: Nuno Almeida, Senior Product Designer at Nagarro
posts.media: Content Builder: videos written like code, one line per shot, and the range of clips it makes
posts.text: I'm a product designer, and I built the tool that makes our LinkedIn videos. My team at Nagarro does a lot of design system work that nobody outside the team ever sees. Screenshots don't do it justice, and screen recordings are too small on a phone. So, working with Claude, I built Content Builder. We write posts in one text file. It shows each one as it will look on LinkedIn, checks it (length, the "…see more" cut, hype words), and films short captioned clips straight from the real product, zoomed in for phones. The clip in this post was made with it. Designers who can shape their own tools make different work. What would you build if the tool you needed didn't exist? #productdesign #designsystems #ai
posts.notes: Nuno's own post, in Nuno's name. Content Builder is in content-builder/ (built with Claude Code).
